name: The Stroop Effect
statement: Naming the ink colour of a word is slow and error-prone when the word spells a different colour.
statementAccent: slow and error-prone when the word spells a different colour
meaning: The Stroop effect is a phenomenon in cognitive psychology demonstrating interference in reaction time. When the name of a colour is printed in an ink colour that does not match the word, for example the word red printed in blue ink, naming the ink colour takes longer and produces more errors than when the word and ink colour match or for neutral stimuli. Reading the word red printed in red is easy, but naming the blue ink of the word red is hard, because the meaning of the word conflicts with the colour to be named. The effect is named after the American psychologist John Ridley Stroop, who published the classic study in 1935, though the phenomenon had earlier antecedents. Because it produces a robust, easily measured slowdown that indexes the conflict between automatic and controlled mental processes, the Stroop task has become one of the most widely used paradigms in all of psychology.
mechanism: The leading explanation is the automaticity of reading. For literate adults, reading is a highly practiced, fast, and largely involuntary process, so when a colour word is presented, its meaning is retrieved automatically whether or not one intends to read it. Naming the ink colour, by contrast, is a slower and more effortful, controlled process. When the word names a different colour than the ink, the automatically retrieved word meaning conflicts with the response required by the ink colour, and this conflict must be resolved, which slows the response and increases errors. Related accounts describe the same conflict in other terms: a speed-of-processing account notes that words are read faster than colours are named, so the word interferes; a selective-attention account holds that naming the ink colour demands more attention than reading; and parallel-processing models attribute the interference to the stronger, more practiced reading pathway overriding the weaker colour-naming one. All converge on the idea that an automatic process interferes with a controlled one.

examples.text: Naming the ink colour of the word red printed in blue is markedly slower than naming the colour when word and ink agree or for neutral stimuli.
Reading is so practiced that the word's meaning is retrieved involuntarily, conflicting with the effortful task of naming a mismatched ink colour.
A variant substitutes emotionally charged words for colour words, used to study how emotional content captures attention and slows colour naming.

variants.name: The automaticity account
variants.text: The leading explanation that reading is automatic and involuntary, so the word meaning conflicts with the controlled task of naming the ink colour.

variants.name: The emotional Stroop task
variants.text: A variant using emotionally salient words in place of colour words to probe attentional capture by emotional content.

whyItMatters: The Stroop effect is one of the most famous and widely used phenomena in psychology, prized as a clean, reliable demonstration of cognitive interference and of the tension between automatic and controlled mental processes. The Stroop task has become a standard tool for measuring selective attention, cognitive control, processing speed, and the ability to inhibit a prepotent response, making it central to research on executive function. It is used clinically and in neuropsychological assessment, since altered interference effects appear in conditions affecting attention and control, and its emotional variant probes how emotionally charged information captures attention. The effect vividly illustrates that skilled processes like reading become automatic and hard to suppress, a key insight into how practice shapes the mind. Simple to run yet deeply informative, the Stroop paradigm has generated an enormous literature and remains a cornerstone method across cognitive, clinical, and developmental psychology.

limits: The Stroop effect is highly robust but depends on the participant being a fluent reader, since the interference stems from automatic reading; it is weaker or absent in those who cannot read the words or in unfamiliar scripts. The exact size of the effect varies with the stimuli, the response mode, and individual differences in attention and cognitive control, and the precise interpretation among competing accounts, automaticity, speed of processing, selective attention, and parallel processing, remains debated even as all point to automatic-versus-controlled conflict. The task measures interference and control under specific conditions rather than a single fixed trait. So the Stroop effect reliably demonstrates cognitive interference and is a valuable measure of attention and control, while the fine details of its mechanism and the interpretation of individual scores require care.
misreadings: The Stroop effect is not about people being unable to see colours; it is that the automatically read word meaning interferes with naming a mismatched ink colour. It is not merely a curiosity but a widely used index of selective attention and cognitive control. And the interference reflects the automaticity of reading rather than a general slowness, so treating the effect as a simple perception problem, or the Stroop task as measuring one fixed ability, misreads a phenomenon that reveals the conflict between automatic and controlled processing.
origin: Named after the American psychologist John Ridley Stroop, who published the classic study Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions in 1935, though the phenomenon had earlier antecedents.
